context.transcript_excerpt: Hello and welcome to the Freight Flow Advisor Brief. This past week, I got the opportunity to travel to Long Beach for the IANA Intermodal Expo. During this expo, there were three conversations that kept coming back to the same question. Can freight actually move when the supply chain says it should? Now, on day one, that question showed up in the gap between a container that is cleared by customs and a container that is physically available to move. Then on day two, it showed up in a rail merger debate between BNSF CEO Katie Farmer and Union Pacific CEO Jim Venna. Now, the premise behind that debate was, does rail win more freight from trucking through stronger collaboration and more shipper choice? Or does it win through consolidation and fewer handoffs? Lastly, it showed up in the exhibit hall where AI, cyber risk, cargo theft, asset intelligence and automation were not theoretical topics. There were central conversations about how freight companies can see problems earlier. They can protect equipment, reduce delay and make the physical system work better. This episode is a recap of those conversations and what they mean for the people who buy, move, manage, and invest in freight. So let's start with what IANA is and why it matters. IANA is the Intermodal Association of North America. It is the industry association representing the combined interest of the intermodal freight community. We're talking about railroads, motor carriers, dredge providers, ocean carriers, ports, chassis providers, equipment owners, technology firms, and the list goes on. Now, simply defined, intermodal freight means moving cargo across more than one transportation mode, most often ship, rail, and truck, while keeping that cargo in the same container or trailer. The objective is really simple. Use each mode where it has a strategic advantage while minimizing the delay, handling costs and risk that occur every time freight changes hands. IANA Intermodal Expo is where that full ecosystem comes together. It is a working marketplace for people who operate the equipment, manage the terminals and dispatch the trucks. It's essentially all of the services that keep North American supply chains moving. That is why the conversations at IANA matter beyond rail or ports alone. You see, a delay at a terminal can become a missed drainage appointment. A chassis shortage can become a missed rail cutoff and a poor rate response can keep freight on the highway. Not to mention a cyber event or theft event that can completely disrupt inventory, insurance, and customer service. So with all of that in context, let's start with the most practical operational lesson that I learned on day one. I think the most important takeaway was also easy to miss. A container may be cleared by customs, but that does not necessarily mean it's ready for a trucker or a railroad or a consignee to move. You see, a container can have its regulatory release. The paperwork can show it as clear. But physically, the container may still be buried in a stack or blocked by other equipment staged in the wrong place or otherwise inaccessible when a driver arrives. That is the difference between cleared and movable. Cleared is a regulatory status. Movable is an operational readiness and the supply chain moves equipment, not documents. Now, that point came into focus during a question and answer session with Michael Rutherford. He's the first assistant secretary for multimodal freight infrastructure and policy at the U.S. Department of Transportation. Now, his office has a broad remit that includes freight policy, data sharing, grant programs, research, cross-modal coordination, and cargo security. The practical question was whether trusted trade data could be used earlier in the process to help terminals make smarter placement decisions before a cleared box becomes a retrieval problem. pending_qa.q: What are the two competing strategies for how rail should win more freight from trucking?
pending_qa.r: BNSF CEO Katie Farmer argued that rail must win through stronger collaboration, commercial responsiveness, and shipper optionality—meaning the ability to choose among railroads with commercially viable routes and negotiating leverage. Union Pacific CEO Jim Vena argued that rail must win through consolidation, fewer handoffs, and a seamless single-line rail product that eliminates multi-carrier complexity.

pending_qa.q: What specific operational problem did Union Pacific identify in the Norfolk Southern to Union Pacific corridor from Harrisburg, Pennsylvania to Salt Lake City?
pending_qa.r: Today, a container can move by Norfolk Southern to Chicago, be unloaded at Norfolk Southern's 47th Street Terminal, trucked roughly 20 miles to Union Pacific's Global 2 Terminal, reloaded, and sent west on Union Pacific. Union Pacific says that process can add up to 36 hours of transit time. A combined railroad would replace that lift, dray, and reload with a block swap in Chicago, projecting a 20-24-hour transit improvement.

pending_qa.q: What does Oliver Wyman's 2025 shipper survey reveal about why shippers are shifting freight from rail to truck?
pending_qa.r: Oliver Wyman's 2025 shipper survey found that at least half of shippers actively shifting freight from rail to truck cited lack of railroad responsiveness as a main reason. The survey also found that pricing is a critical modal decision factor and that shippers remain frustrated by the complexity and slow commercial response.

pending_qa.q: How does BlackBerry Radar combine equipment data to improve operational decision-making in intermodal logistics?
pending_qa.r: BlackBerry Radar helps transportation operators combine equipment location, activity, and condition data with business information so teams can identify priorities and act more proactively. The platform provides utilization data based on start-stop movements, geofences for detention and dwell time, and integrates with YMS, TMS, UMS systems and ELD providers to support maintenance scheduling and yard checks.

pending_qa.q: What specific performance improvement did BlackBerry Radar achieve in its work with DCLI?
pending_qa.r: BlackBerry Radar reduced inspection lead time by 33% in its work with DCLI, and DCLI intends to incorporate Radar across 100,000 units. This demonstrates how asset intelligence—not merely knowing where a unit is, but using that information to get the right equipment in front of the right team—delivers practical operational value.

pending_qa.q: What are the key deployment conditions for Field AI's physical autonomy software in freight environments?
pending_qa.r: Field AI's autonomy software is designed to help robots operate in real-world, unstructured environments where GPS can fail, layouts change, and people move through the space. The software enables autonomous systems to understand uncertainty and perform useful work without needing a perfectly mapped and controlled environment. For freight, this points toward use cases such as automated inspection, site patrols, anomaly detection, yard monitoring, and repetitive work that is difficult to staff.

pending_qa.q: What deadlines apply to parties seeking formal status in the Surface Transportation Board review of the proposed Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern merger?
pending_qa.r: Interested stakeholders who want formal party of record status have until September 30th, 2026 to file a notice of intent to participate. Comments, protests, requests for conditions, and other opposition filings are due November 18th, 2026.
